title: Cross the Flooding Grid
statement:
An n × n grid holds the height of each square of land, grid[r][c]. All heights are different, and they are exactly the numbers 0 to n² − 1.

Water rises over time: at time t the water level is t, and you can stand on a square only when its height is at most t. You may move between squares that share a side, as many as you like and instantly, as long as both are at most the water level. You may wait anywhere for as long as you like.

You start on the top-left square and want to reach the bottom-right one. Return the earliest time at which that is possible.

examples.why: Going right along the top costs 7 at best, with the smallest total height (0 + 1 + 7 + 3 + 2). Down the left side and along the bottom (0, 6, 4, 5, 2) has a larger sum but never goes above 6.
You cannot even stand on the start square until time 3. Ignoring the start square's own height gives 2.
The route winds around the border. Every shortcut through the middle climbs to 10 or more.

constraints: The heights are a rearrangement of 0, 1, …, n² − 1
hints: The time you need for a given route is the highest square on it. So you want the route whose highest square is as low as possible, not the route with the smallest sum.
If you can cross at time t, you can also cross at any later time. That monotone yes/no question can be binary searched, with a flood fill to answer each guess.

Or adapt Dijkstra: the "distance" of a square is the lowest possible maximum height on a route to it. Extending a route to a neighbour gives max(current, neighbour height). Always expand the square with the smallest value from a min-heap.

explain.intuition:
A route is usable at time t exactly when every square on it is at most t. So the time a route needs is its highest square, and the answer is the smallest possible "highest square" over all routes. This is a minimax path problem.

Dijkstra still works when you change what a path costs. Here a path's cost is the maximum height on it, and extending a path never lowers that maximum. That is the same property that non-negative weights give ordinary Dijkstra, so "the unsettled square with the smallest cost is final" still holds. Pop the lowest square from a min-heap, and push each unvisited neighbour with cost max(cost, height). The first time the bottom-right square comes out of the heap, its cost is the answer.

A second view: the answer is a time t, and "can I cross at time t?" switches from no to yes once and stays yes. Binary search on t, answering each guess with a BFS over squares of height at most t.
steps: Push (grid[0][0], 0, 0) onto a min-heap and mark the start as seen.
Pop the entry (level, r, c) with the lowest level.
If (r, c) is the bottom-right square, return level.
For each unseen neighbour, mark it seen and push (max(level, its height), neighbour).
A square is pushed once, because the first push already comes from the lowest level that can reach it at that moment, and levels only grow.
pitfalls: Minimising the sum of heights, as ordinary shortest path does. Example 1 is built so that the lowest-sum route needs time 7.
Forgetting that the start square counts. Example 2 needs time 3 just to stand on it.
Moving greedily to the lowest neighbour without a heap. You can get pulled into a low pocket and never consider a better branch you passed earlier.

solutions.title: Try every time in order
solutions.idea: For t = 0, 1, 2, …, flood fill from the start over squares of height at most t. Return the first t at which the fill reaches the bottom-right.

solutions.title: Binary search on the time
solutions.idea: Crossing at time t is possible for every t from the answer upward. Binary search for the first yes, using a BFS over squares of height at most t.

solutions.title: Dijkstra on the highest square
solutions.idea: A route's cost is its highest square. Expand squares from a min-heap ordered by that cost; the first time the target comes out, its cost is the answer.

followups: Since the heights are exactly 0 to n² − 1, you can flood the squares in height order and stop when start and end join. Which structure tells you when they are in the same region?
Heights may repeat and are not limited to n² − 1. Which of the three solutions still works unchanged?
